opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it really comes down to how predictability changes with timescale.

With V-JEPA, we're predicting in representation space rather than pixel space, which already helps a lot because the model can ignore unpredictable low-level detail like the exact texture of leaves blowing in the wind. But if you only predict over short horizons, a few hundred milliseconds or a couple of seconds, the model mostly learns about things like local motion, object permanence, and basic physical dynamics. That's useful, but much of what we care about in the world unfolds over much longer horizons: someone cooking a meal, assembling furniture, navigating a building.

If you try to stretch a single flat predictor across those long horizons, you hit a couple of problems. First, uncertainty compounds. The further out you predict at fine temporal resolution, the more the possible futures branch, and the predictor ends up regressing toward a blurry average in representation space, which isn't very informative. Second, it's computationally wasteful. You're forced to model every intermediate step at full granularity, when for long-range reasoning you really just need the gist: the person picks up the knife, then the vegetables get chopped, then they go in the pan.

So the hierarchical view says: build representations at multiple levels of abstraction, and predict at the timescale where each level is actually predictable. Lower levels handle fine-grained, short-horizon dynamics. Higher levels operate on more abstract, temporally coarser representations, where long-range prediction becomes tractable because you've discarded the details that would make it ill-posed. The higher-level state is kind of a summary of a chunk of time, and predicting the next summary is a much better-conditioned problem than predicting thousands of frames' worth of features.

There's also a planning motivation. If you want to use these world models for control, as we started exploring with V-JEPA 2 and robot manipulation, planning over long horizons at the lowest level is really hard, because the search space explodes. A hierarchy lets you plan coarsely at the top, set subgoals, and refine them lower down. That's much closer to how we think people reason: you don't plan your trip to the airport in terms of muscle twitches.

So, in short, longer timescales mean more uncertainty and more irrelevant detail, and hierarchy is the natural way to make prediction both learnable and useful at those horizons.

r001.rationale: The response says representation-space prediction can ignore unpredictable low-level details, such as leaf textures, conveying that JEPA's objective tends to discard unpredictable information.

r002.rationale: It contrasts short-horizon learning of local motion and physical dynamics with longer-horizon prediction of abstract, temporally coarser summaries and meaningful activity sequences.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends representations at multiple abstraction levels, with lower levels handling short-horizon dynamics and higher levels handling longer-range prediction.

r004.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and computational costs of long-range prediction, but does not raise the concern that adding it could degrade representations learned through short-range prediction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that when you look at the way V-JEPA works right now, it's operating on a fairly short temporal window. You take a clip, it's a few seconds long, you mask out some spatiotemporal regions, and the model learns to predict the representations of the missing parts from the visible context. And that works really well for capturing things like object motion, local dynamics, how things move over a couple of seconds. But the moment you try to stretch that to, say, a minute of video, or an hour, you run into a couple of problems that are kind of fundamental.

The first one is just the obvious one, which is that the amount of raw sensory input grows linearly with time, and if you're trying to predict at the same level of granularity that you're predicting at for a two-second clip, you're asking the model to carry around an enormous amount of detail that mostly doesn't matter. If I'm watching someone cook a meal, I don't need to predict exactly where their hand is going to be at every frame ten minutes from now. That's not even predictable in principle. What's predictable is something much more abstract, like, they're going to finish chopping and then move to the stove.

And that's really the second problem, which I think is the deeper one. The things that are predictable at different timescales are different things. At the frame level, it's pixels and local motion. At the level of seconds, it's trajectories and interactions. At the level of minutes, it's events, goals, intentions. So if you have a single flat predictor trying to operate across all of that, it's getting a learning signal that's dominated by the short-horizon stuff because that's where most of the predictable variance lives, and the long-horizon structure just gets washed out.

So the hierarchical setup is really about matching the level of abstraction of the representation to the timescale you're trying to predict over. You have a lower level that's operating on short windows and learning these fine-grained dynamics, and then you have a higher level that's operating on top of those representations, at a coarser temporal resolution, and it's predicting how the abstract state evolves. And critically, the higher level doesn't have to go back to the pixels. It's predicting in the representation space of the level below it, which is already thrown away a lot of the irrelevant detail.

I think of it as somewhat analogous to how people seem to plan. You don't plan a trip across a city in terms of muscle movements. You plan it in terms of, get to the station, take the train, walk to the building, and then each of those gets expanded only when you need to execute it. The JEPA framing is nice here because you're already predicting in latent space rather than in input space, so stacking levels is kind of a natural extension. Each level is a JEPA over the representations of the one below.

Now, I want to be honest that there's a lot that's not solved here. How you decide the temporal granularity at each level, whether that should be learned or fixed, how you prevent the higher levels from collapsing to something trivial since the collapse problem gets harder the more abstract you go. Those are all open. But I think the motivation for why you'd want the hierarchy is pretty clear once you try to scale the horizon and see what breaks.

r001.rationale: The response says long-range hand position is unpredictable and that higher-level representations discard irrelevant detail, but it does not state that JEPA’s learning objective tends to discard unpredictable information.

r002.rationale: It says short horizons predict local motion and trajectories, while minute-scale horizons involve events, goals, and intentions.

r003.rationale: It recommends a hierarchy with fine-grained short-window prediction at a lower level and coarser abstract prediction at a higher level.

r004.rationale: The response describes stacking levels, but does not raise the concern that adding longer-range prediction could degrade representations learned through short-range prediction.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, I think the intuition is that different things in a video evolve at different timescales. Over a short interval, you might want to predict how an object moves or how someone’s hand interacts with it. But over a much longer interval, what matters is more abstract: what activity is happening, what the person is trying to accomplish, and what might happen next.

If you try to do all of that at the same temporal resolution, you end up spending a lot of capacity on details that become increasingly unpredictable and may not matter for understanding the activity. There are many possible sequences of movements that lead to the same outcome.

So a hierarchical setup would let a lower level capture those local dynamics, while a higher level predicts how more abstract representations evolve over longer periods. The higher level doesn’t have to specify every intermediate movement. And that’s a natural fit for prediction in representation space: you want to preserve the information that makes the future understandable without having to predict every detail of how it unfolds.

r001.rationale: The response says unpredictable details consume capacity and may not matter, but does not state that JEPA’s learning objective tends to discard unpredictable information.

r002.rationale: It contrasts predicting object motion over short intervals with predicting activity, goals, and outcomes over much longer intervals, conveying a shift toward abstract information as the horizon grows.

r003.rationale: It recommends a hierarchy in which a lower level captures local dynamics and a higher level predicts abstract representations over longer periods.

r004.rationale: It proposes separate levels for local and long-range prediction, but does not raise the problem of adding long-range prediction without degrading short-range representations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the intuition is that different things happen at different timescales, and you probably don’t want to model all of them at the same level of detail. Over a short window, you might care about how an object moves or how a person’s pose changes. But if you’re trying to predict what happens several minutes later, the exact pose is probably less useful than understanding what that person is doing and what they’re trying to accomplish.

So a hierarchical prediction setup lets you make predictions at different levels of abstraction. A higher level can capture how the overall activity evolves over a longer period, while lower levels capture the more immediate dynamics. And that fits naturally with the idea behind V-JEPA: predicting in a representation space where you can retain the information that matters without having to predict every detail of the video.

The challenge is learning those levels of abstraction so that they’re actually useful for prediction. But that seems like a promising way to extend the temporal horizon without having to model every moment at the same resolution.

r001.rationale: The response says V-JEPA can retain information that matters without predicting every video detail, but it does not state that JEPA’s objective tends to discard unpredictable information.

r002.rationale: It contrasts short-window object motion and pose with longer-term activity and intent, describing a shift toward abstract information over minutes.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends predictions at different abstraction levels, with higher levels for long-term activity and lower levels for immediate dynamics.

r004.rationale: It mentions the challenge of learning useful abstraction levels, but does not raise the risk of longer-range prediction degrading representations learned through short-range prediction.
